corpusNote: Epicurus was enormously prolific — Diogenes Laertius X.26 calls him the most productive of all philosophers and credits him with about 300 rolls — yet almost the entire output is lost. What survives intact is a deliberately curated survival kit: three summary letters and two sets of maxims, transmitted because Epicureanism was a memorisation-based doctrine and these were its catechism. Diogenes Laertius Book X preserves the letters and the Principal Doctrines whole; the Vatican Sayings surfaced in a manuscript in 1888; and the great treatise On Nature is being physically recovered, book by book, from the carbonised scrolls of the Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum — a corpus still slowly growing under new imaging technology.

works.title: On Nature

date.note: Composed over much of Epicurus' career; individual books can sometimes be relatively dated.

works.extent: Epicurus' magnum opus, in 37 books — and mostly lost. Substantial charred fragments of several books (notably II, XI, XIV, XV, XXV, XXVIII) survive among the Herculaneum papyri from the Villa of the Papyri, recovered since the 18th century and still being read with multispectral and X-ray imaging.
works.transmission: Uniquely among major lost works, On Nature is being physically recovered. Piso's villa at Herculaneum — the library of the Epicurean Philodemus — was buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE; its carbonised scrolls, excavated from 1752, include copies of Epicurus' own On Nature. Book XXVIII carries a colophon dating it to the archonship of Nicias (c. 296/295 BCE), giving Epicurus' own words verbatim. The Vesuvius Challenge (2023– ) has begun reading unopened scrolls by CT scanning and AI, so this corpus is expected to keep expanding.
works.authenticity: Genuine. The papyrus fragments are Epicurus' own text, our only substantial verbatim access to his physics beyond the summary Letter to Herodotus.
works.summary: The full exposition of Epicurean physics that the Letter to Herodotus condenses: atoms and void as the only per se existents; the infinity of atoms and worlds; the properties and 'minimal parts' of atoms; the atomic swerve (clinamen) underwriting free will; the mortality of the soul (itself atomic); the theory of perception by films of atoms (eidōla); the critique of determinism (Bk XXV on 'what depends on us'); and the naturalistic account of the origin of language and society. Lucretius' De Rerum Natura is essentially this work put into Latin verse.
editions: Arrighetti, Epicuro: Opere (1973); Leone, Millot, and others for individual books (La Scuola di Epicuro series)
translations: Selected fragments in Long & Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers (1987); Inwood & Gerson, The Epicurus Reader (1994)
works.notes: The single best living example of a philosophical corpus still under recovery — worth flagging in the atlas as a text whose extent changes with technology (the 2023– Vesuvius Challenge reads).

works.title: Letter to Herodotus
works.extent: Complete, preserved in Diogenes Laertius X.35–83.
works.transmission: Preserved whole within Diogenes Laertius' Life of Epicurus.
works.summary: Epicurus' own summary (epitomē) of his physics, written for students to memorise: the principles of atomism (nothing comes from nothing; the universe is bodies and void, both infinite); atomic properties and motion; the plurality of worlds; the atomic soul and its mortality; perception by eidōla; the goal of removing the fear of the gods and of death through natural explanation. The doctrinal core of the physics in portable form.
translations: Inwood & Gerson, The Epicurus Reader (1994); Bailey, Epicurus: The Extant Remains (1926, public domain); Hicks, Loeb (1925)

works.title: Letter to Pythocles
works.extent: Complete, preserved in Diogenes Laertius X.84–116.
works.transmission: Within Diogenes Laertius X. Some scholars think it an epitome compiled by a pupil from Epicurus' On Nature rather than a letter Epicurus penned, but it transmits his doctrine.
works.authenticity: Genuine in substance; possibly a school digest of Epicurus' meteorology.
works.summary: A summary of celestial and atmospheric phenomena (meteōra): the size of the sun, phases of the moon, eclipses, weather, comets. The methodological heart is the doctrine of 'multiple explanations' — where several natural accounts are equally compatible with the phenomena, all should be accepted, since dogmatic single explanations reintroduce the anxiety and superstition Epicureanism exists to dispel.

works.title: Letter to Menoeceus
works.extent: Complete, preserved in Diogenes Laertius X.122–135.
works.transmission: Within Diogenes Laertius X. The best preserved and most read of the three letters.
works.summary: Epicurus' ethics in miniature: philosophy is medicine for the soul at every age; the 'tetrapharmakos' (fourfold cure) — the gods are not to be feared, death is nothing to us ('when we exist death is not present, and when death is present we do not exist'), the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to endure; the classification of desires (natural and necessary / natural and unnecessary / empty); pleasure as the absence of bodily pain (aponia) and mental disturbance (ataraxia) — not sensualism; and prudence (phronēsis) as the greatest good and root of all virtues. The founding statement of Epicurean ethics.
translations: Inwood & Gerson (1994); Bailey (1926, public domain); Hicks, Loeb (1925)

works.title: Principal Doctrines (Sovereign Maxims)
works.extent: Complete: 40 numbered maxims, preserved in Diogenes Laertius X.139–154.
works.transmission: Preserved as the capstone of Diogenes Laertius' Life. Quoted also by Cicero and Philodemus, confirming the collection's early canonical status.
works.authenticity: Genuine (a curated selection from Epicurus' works, possibly assembled by the school).
works.summary: Forty aphorisms distilling the doctrine for memorisation: KD 1 (the blessed and imperishable being feels no anger or favour — so no fear of the gods); KD 2 (death is nothing to us); KD 3–4 (the limits of pleasure and pain); KD 5 (the unity of the pleasant life with the virtuous); and the famous social maxims KD 31–38 on justice as a contract of mutual advantage ('there is no such thing as justice in the abstract; it is a compact... neither to harm nor be harmed'). The doctrinal skeleton of Epicureanism.

works.title: Vatican Sayings (Gnomologium Vaticanum Epicureum)

date.note: The compilation is later; the individual sayings are Epicurus' and his immediate circle's.

works.extent: 81 sayings, discovered in 1888 in a 14th-century manuscript (Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1950).
works.transmission: Unknown to the mediaeval and early-modern reception of Epicurus; found by C. Wotke in the Vatican Library in 1888 — a modern addition to the corpus. Some sayings overlap with the Principal Doctrines; others are attributable to Epicurus' associates Metrodorus and Hermarchus.
works.authenticity: Largely genuine Epicurean material; a minority are by other early Epicureans, and the collection is a later anthology.
works.summary: A wider and more personal range than the Principal Doctrines, including sayings on friendship — the school's signature value: 'Of the things wisdom provides for the blessedness of one's whole life, by far the greatest is the possession of friendship' (SV 27); 'It is not so much the help of friends as the confidence of their help that we need' (SV 34); and reflections on gratitude, self-sufficiency, and the wise person's freedom from anxiety.
works.notes: Like the Herculaneum On Nature, a reminder that this corpus grew in modern times — the Vatican Sayings entered it only in 1888.

works.title: Lost works, letters, and the Testament (On the Goal, On Choice and Avoidance, the Kyria, the Will)
works.extent: The bulk of ~300 rolls, lost. Diogenes Laertius X.27–28 lists the 'best' of them by title; the Will/Testament is preserved whole (X.16–21).
citations: DL X.16–22 (the Will, and the Letter on his deathbed to Idomeneus)
works.transmission: Titles preserved in Diogenes' catalogue; the Testament and a few personal letters (to Idomeneus, to his mother, to a child) survive in quotation.
works.summary: Titles include On Nature (above), On Atoms and Void, On the Criterion or Canon (the epistemology of the 'kanōn'), On the Goal (Peri telous, on pleasure as the end), On Choice and Avoidance, On the Gods, On Piety, On Lives, Symposium, and On Sight, Touch, Music, Justice, and more. The Will (X.16–21) endows the school (the Garden) and provides for the memorial celebrations of Epicurus and his friends. The deathbed letter to Idomeneus — written 'on the blessed day which is also the last of my life', amid the agony of kidney-stone and dysentery, yet counting it happy through the memory of past conversations — is one of the most famous documents of ancient philosophy.

works.title: Testimonia (Lucretius, Cicero, Philodemus, Diogenes of Oinoanda)
works.extent: The rich secondary tradition that supplements the thin direct survival.
citations: Cicero, De Finibus I–II, De Natura Deorum I
works.transmission: Lucretius' Latin poem is effectively a lost book of Epicurus recovered in verse; Cicero reports and criticises the ethics and theology; Philodemus' Herculaneum library preserves Epicurean philosophy of the 1st c. BCE; and Diogenes of Oinoanda (2nd c. CE) carved an entire Epicurean summa onto a stoa wall in Lycia — the largest ancient inscription, still being excavated.
works.authenticity: Not by Epicurus; indispensable for reconstructing the doctrine given how little of his own writing survives.
works.summary: The channels through which Epicureanism actually reached posterity before the papyri: Lucretius for the physics, Cicero for the ethics and its critics, Philodemus for the later school, Diogenes of Oinoanda for a public monumental exposition.
editions: Usener, Epicurea (1887); Smith, Diogenes of Oinoanda: The Epicurean Inscription (1993)
translations: Long & Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers (1987); Inwood & Gerson (1994)
works.notes: Cross-link to lucretius (De Rerum Natura is the fullest surviving Epicurean physics).

sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives Book X (verified: 37 books of On Nature, three letters, Principal Doctrines, Will)
